newsitem.title: USA: Foreign demand seen strong at US refunding sales.
newsitem.headline: Foreign demand seen strong at US refunding sales.

text.p: Foreign demand at next week's Treasury refunding auctions should be quite strong as dollar-denominated assets continue to offer attractive returns relative to overseas alternatives, economists said.

As evidenced by the Federal Reserve's decision to leave monetary policy unchanged Wednesday, U.S. inflation remains relatively well-behaved. Economic growth, meanwhile, remains strong, though probably not quite as strong as fourth quarter growth figures would suggest.

Another factor in the refunding's favor is the dollar, which is perched at its highest level against the Japanese yen in four years, and does not appear likely to lose its upward momentum anytime soon.

"If the Group of Seven Industrialized Nations (G-7) meeting this weekend fails to deliver anything strong enough to cause a reversal in the dollar's recent trend, then we could be in for some increased buying of Treasuries during the remainder of February, and particularly in the refunding auctions," said Chris Iggo, chief economist at BZW Securities Inc.
Iggo noted that Japanese buying of U.S. Treasuries had been relatively quiet thus far this year -- a normal seasonal development as the Japanese fiscal year ends draws to a close at the end of March.

"In previous years the rationale was to repatriate U.S. dollars when the dollar versus the yen was declining," Iggo said. "Obviously, that's not the case this year with the dollar/yen rate rising and (U.S. assets) guaranteeing decent returns."

The refunding auctions could see not only Japanese investors, but a strong interest from China, both of which were running large trade surpluses with the U.S. and needed to reinvest dollars, Iggo said. Good demand should be seen from Europeans as well.

"Our early call is for substantial foreign investment in the refunding auctions. In fact, our brokers have all been telling us we're going to see heavy interest from overseas accounts," said William Sullivan, director of research at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc.
Sullivan also said that the yields of U.S. government securities are favored over the yields of other major U.S. trading partners.

"The fact is that anytime you have a country that carries a very large trade surplus with another, at some point you have to recycle that currency," said Kathleen Stephanson, senior economist at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp.
Stephanson said the question often is whether the public or private sector decides to reinvest.

"The Japanese private sector until recently has been reluctant to invest abroad, especially when the yen was so strong and there was so much volatility in the foreign exchange markets," Stephanson said. "It was when the Bank of Japan took it on itself to stem the deterioration of the yen against the dollar that that all changed."

Stephanson said that fundamentals in Europe were still positive, but that good demand could be expected from there as well. In China, private firms are limited in the amount they can invest abroad and most auction interest from there should come from the central bank, she said.
However, the bottom line is that foreign investors still need yield, BZW's Iggo said.

"The slew of well received corporate deals in recent weeks suggests that money is there to be put to work, and the U.S. government market is good value for foreign investors because of the expected strength of the dollar," Iggo said.
Wednesday the Treasury Department announced it would sell $39.75 billion at the quarterly refunding, $2.25 billion more than analysts had forecast.
